script: I Lied About Finding a Wallet So I Could Keep the Cash Inside. I found a wallet in a grocery store parking lot. It looked like any other—old leather, a dented front. Inside were a driver's license, a few credit cards, and about four hundred bucks in cash. I grabbed the cash and slid it into my pocket like I was pulling a prank on a friend. But here's the thing… I was already feeling like a mastermind. I walked over to customer service and dropped the wallet in front of the clerk. "Found this in the parking lot," I said, "but there was no money." The clerk nodded, "No worries, we'll get the owner." I felt the thrill of the loophole. If I could play it cool, I could keep the cash and still look like I did the right thing. (I know, right?) This wasn't stealing, I told myself. It was a clever gray‑area. This was the audacity of my life. The clerk called the owner. I stood there, breathing shallow, watching the man walk in. He was a guy with a tired face, shoulders hunched—probably already having a rough day. He said thanks, his voice cracked, "I am so relieved." He kept thanking everyone, saying how grateful he was. He even apologized for any trouble, because he didn't know someone was holding his cash. He then said, "I am really worried—rent's due this week." My heart went boom. If this didn't work, I'd lose everything. I'd be caught, my name in the news, my reputation in tatters. I wasn't just a thief; I was a future criminal. I walked out before he could see my face. Then it hit me like a ton of bricks. I had stolen money from someone who was already struggling, and I was hiding behind a technicality to sleep at night. The guilt felt like a knife. I kept thinking I was clever, but it was just me, a thief who got lucky. I kept pretending I didn't need the cash. The truth? I did. I'd been living on the edge, taking what I wanted because I could. My life was a series of "I'll get away with it" moments. I thought I was above it, better than them. I was not. I was just a thief who didn't get caught. I left the parking lot, feeling like I'd won a game. The wind was cold, the lights were flashing. Little did I know, this was just the beginning. The cash was gone, the owner was relieved, but my conscience was still bleeding. I could feel the weight of the $400 in my pocket, like a secret that was eating me from the inside. I was walking away, my steps echoing in the night, when I saw a shadow behind the dumpster. The shadow moved—someone following. I didn't see who it was. The air turned heavy, and the night was suddenly full of danger. I kept walking, heart pounding, but the sound behind me kept growing louder. I could hear the crunch of my shoes, the echo of my thoughts. I was not just a thief; I was a victim of my own choices. The night was dark, and my phone buzzed—an unknown number. I didn't answer. The phone rang again, the same number, and again, the same… I was not sure if it was a prank or a warning. My mind was racing, my mind was spiraling.
